definition: The process of formally verifying and vouching for the integrity, configuration, or compliance status of a system, component, or claim, often producing a signed statement that a relying party can check (e.g., remote attestation confirming a device's firmware or boot state hasn't been tampered with).
examContext: Know attestation can refer to a device cryptographically proving its boot or configuration integrity (remote attestation) or to a vendor formally vouching for compliance with a security standard; both appear in identity and third-party risk scenarios.
analogy: Like a notary stamping a document to formally certify 'I verified this is genuine,' giving anyone who sees the stamp a trustworthy, checkable claim without redoing the verification themselves.
relatedTerms: Due diligence, Due care, Governance, Digital signature, Non-repudiation

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's team enables remote attestation on all corporate laptops so that before a device can connect to the VPN, it must cryptographically prove its boot process and firmware haven't been modified, automatically blocking any laptop that fails the integrity check.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud customer wants proof that a virtual machine booted with the expected firmware and bootloader and has not been tampered with, before the machine is allowed to receive secrets. Which of the following BEST provides this proof?
quizOptions: A) Single sign-on, in which the user's identity provider issues a signed assertion to each app
B) Remote attestation, in which the device presents a signed measurement of its boot state
C) Code obfuscation, in which the application's logic is made difficult to read
D) Certificate pinning, in which the client accepts only a specific known certificate
detail.explanation: Remote attestation lets a device cryptographically prove its boot or configuration state to a relying party, often through a TPM-signed measurement. SSO asserts user identity, obfuscation hides code, and pinning restricts which certificate is trusted.

items.name: People
items.detail: Passwords and PINs, biometrics, smart cards and tokens, security keys, authenticator apps, MFA.

items.name: Systems and devices
items.detail: Machine certificates, 802.1X/NAC, device attestation (TPM measured boot), service accounts and API keys/secrets, IPsec certificates or pre-shared keys.

items.name: Mutual authentication
items.detail: BOTH sides prove who they are (EAP-TLS, mutual TLS, Kerberos), which defeats rogue servers and impersonation.

items.name: Internal
items.detail: Performed by the organization's own staff (an internal audit team or audit committee). Good for readiness and compliance checks; less independent.

items.name: External
items.detail: Performed by an independent third party or a regulator. More objective and credible.

items.name: Self-assessment
items.detail: The organization reviews its own controls against a checklist. Cheap and quick, but the least objective.

items.name: Regulatory examination
items.detail: An audit required by law or a regulator.

items.name: Independent third-party audit
items.detail: An outside auditor attests that controls work (for example a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification).

items.name: Attestation
items.detail: A formal statement from an auditor or responsible party that controls are as described.

definition: An access control model that grants or denies access by evaluating a combination of attributes about the subject, the object, and the environment (such as job title, data sensitivity, device health, time of day, and location) against policy rules, rather than relying on a single fixed role.
examContext: Expect ABAC to be contrasted with RBAC on the exam: ABAC evaluates multiple attributes (user, resource, environment) for fine-grained, context-aware decisions, while RBAC grants access based on a single assigned role.
analogy: Like a nightclub bouncer who checks your age, the dress code, whether you're on the guest list, and how late it is before deciding to let you in, not just whether you hold a 'VIP' card.
relatedTerms: Role-based access control, Mandatory access control, Discretionary access control, Rule-based access control, Zero trust

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the company's cloud access management platform so that finance employees can only open the payroll application when they are on a corporate-managed laptop, connecting from inside the country, and during normal business hours; anyone missing even one attribute is denied automatically.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital wants a doctor to read a patient's chart only if the doctor works in the patient's department, is on duty, is using a managed device and is inside the hospital network. Which of the following access control models BEST supports these context-aware rules?
quizOptions: A) Role-based access control, which grants access according to one assigned job role
B) Discretionary access control, in which the owner of each chart decides who may read it
C) Mandatory access control, in which fixed labels on users and objects decide access
D) Attribute-based access control, which evaluates user, resource and environment attributes
detail.explanation: ABAC combines attributes of the user, the resource and the environment, such as department, duty status, device and location, into policy decisions. RBAC uses a single role, DAC leaves decisions to owners, and MAC relies on fixed labels.

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: The process of verifying that an entity, such as a user, device, or system, is who or what it claims to be.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes authentication, which proves identity, from authorization, which grants access; expect factor-based questions covering knowledge, possession, and inherence.
analogy: Like showing your ID badge at a building's front desk before anyone decides what floors you can visit.
relatedTerms: Authorization, Multifactor authentication, Biometrics, Single sign-on, Accountability

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures a VPN login to require a password plus a push notification to the employee's phone, confirming the user's identity before any resources are reached.
detail.quizQuestion: A user enters a valid username and a correct password, and the system confirms who the user is. The user then tries to open the payroll folder and is denied. Which of the following BEST describes what happened?
quizOptions: A) Authentication failed, and authorization then failed to grant access to the folder
B) Authentication succeeded, and non-repudiation prevented the user from opening the folder
C) Authentication succeeded, and authorization failed to grant access to the folder
D) Authentication succeeded, and accounting failed to record the user's sign-in
detail.explanation: Verifying the user's identity is authentication, and it succeeded. Being denied access to a resource is an authorization decision based on permissions. Accounting records activity, and non-repudiation proves that actions occurred.

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: Length
items.detail: The strongest single factor against guessing and cracking. Favor long passphrases over short complex strings.

items.name: Complexity
items.detail: Requires mixed character types. Current NIST guidance prefers length plus a blocklist of known-bad passwords over forced complexity.

items.name: Reuse / history
items.detail: Password history stops users from recycling their last N passwords.

items.name: Expiration / maximum age
items.detail: Forces a change after a set time. Current NIST guidance says do not force routine changes unless there is evidence of compromise.

items.name: Minimum age
items.detail: Stops a user from changing the password repeatedly in one sitting to cycle back to an old one.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Locks the account after N failed attempts. Defeats online brute force, but can be abused to lock out legitimate users (a denial of service).

items.name: Password manager
items.detail: Generates and stores unique strong passwords so users do not reuse them. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

items.name: Passwordless
items.detail: FIDO2 keys, passkeys and biometrics remove the shared secret that attackers phish or crack.

items.name: People
items.detail: Passwords and PINs, biometrics, smart cards and tokens, security keys, authenticator apps, MFA.

items.name: Systems and devices
items.detail: Machine certificates, 802.1X/NAC, device attestation (TPM measured boot), service accounts and API keys/secrets, IPsec certificates or pre-shared keys.

items.name: Mutual authentication
items.detail: BOTH sides prove who they are (EAP-TLS, mutual TLS, Kerberos), which defeats rogue servers and impersonation.

definition: A hardware or software item that generates or stores a credential used to prove identity, such as a key fob showing a rotating code, an authenticator app (TOTP) or an API or session token.
examContext: A hard token is a physical device; a soft token is an app. It is a "something you have" factor. The word "token" also means an access or session token in OAuth, so read the context.
analogy: A rotating-code key fob like the ones banks hand out.
relatedTerms: Multifactor authentication, Security key, Smart card, Single sign-on

detail.practicalScenario: An engineer uses an authenticator app that shows a new six-digit code every 30 seconds. The app is a soft token that proves she holds her registered device.
detail.quizQuestion: A defense contractor must give second-factor tokens to 2,000 employees who work in secure areas where personal phones are not permitted. Which of the following token types is the BEST choice?
quizOptions: A) Hardware tokens, because they are physical devices that do not depend on a phone
B) SMS codes, because they arrive on the employee's phone without any extra software
C) Soft tokens in an authenticator app, because they run on any employee's personal phone
D) Email codes, because they can be read on any computer inside the secure area
detail.explanation: A hard token is a physical something-you-have device that works where phones are banned. Authenticator apps and SMS codes both need a phone, and email codes depend on a mailbox that may itself be protected by weaker authentication.

definition: The process of granting or denying an authenticated entity specific permissions to resources based on policy.
examContext: Exam questions often present a scenario where a user is authenticated but still denied access, testing that you recognize this as an authorization failure rather than an authentication one.
analogy: Like a hotel key card that only opens your assigned room floor, not every door in the building.
relatedTerms: Authentication, Least privilege, Role-based access control, Mandatory access control, Accountability

detail.practicalScenario: Alex sets up role-based permissions so that interns who successfully log into the network can only read shared drive folders, not modify payroll files.
detail.quizQuestion: A new employee signs in successfully but cannot open a shared engineering folder. The help desk confirms that the account is active and the password is correct. Which of the following is the MOST likely issue?
quizOptions: A) The account has not been granted the permissions that the folder requires
B) The employee's workstation is missing the latest antivirus definition updates from the vendor
C) The multifactor authentication token has fallen out of sync with the authentication server
D) The employee's password does not meet the complexity rules of the company's policy
detail.explanation: A successful sign-in with a correct password means authentication worked. Being unable to open the folder is an authorization problem, so the account needs the right permissions. A password or token issue would block the sign-in itself.

definition: Automation uses scripts and tools to perform individual tasks without manual effort; orchestration coordinates many automated tasks and systems into end-to-end workflows, as SOAR platforms do in security operations.
examContext: Benefits: efficiency, enforcing baselines, secure scaling, faster reaction time and a workforce multiplier. Drawbacks: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt and ongoing supportability.
analogy: Automation is a robot that welds one joint; orchestration is the conductor coordinating the whole assembly line.
relatedTerms: SOAR, IaC, Guard rail, Technical debt, Single point of failure

detail.practicalScenario: When the SIEM detects a compromised account, a SOAR playbook automatically disables the account, isolates the laptop, opens a ticket and notifies the analyst, all within seconds.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants a phishing alert to automatically trigger several actions across different tools: extract the URL, check its reputation, delete matching messages from all mailboxes and open a ticket. Which of the following BEST describes this capability?
quizOptions: A) Automation of a single task, which performs one step without any coordination
B) Infrastructure as code, which describes servers and networks in machine-readable files
C) Continuous integration, which merges developers' code changes into a shared repository
D) Orchestration, which coordinates many automated tasks across tools into one workflow
detail.explanation: Orchestration coordinates many automated tasks across tools into an end-to-end workflow, as SOAR platforms do. A single automated task lacks coordination, CI merges code, and IaC defines infrastructure rather than security workflows.

items.name: User provisioning
items.detail: Automatically create, change and remove accounts as people join, move and leave.

items.name: Resource provisioning
items.detail: Spin up servers, networks and cloud resources from code (infrastructure as code).

items.name: Guard rails
items.detail: Automated limits that stop risky actions before they happen.

items.name: Security groups
items.detail: Automatically apply and adjust network access rules.

items.name: Ticket creation and escalation
items.detail: Alerts automatically open tickets and escalate them if unanswered.

items.name: Enabling / disabling services and access
items.detail: Quickly turn services or accounts on or off, such as disabling a compromised account.

items.name: Continuous integration and testing
items.detail: Automatically build and test code on every change to catch problems early.

items.name: Integrations and APIs
items.detail: Connect tools so they share data and trigger each other (SOAR playbooks).

variants.title: Automation and orchestration: benefits and drawbacks

items.name: Efficiency / time saving
items.detail: Routine work is done faster and with less manual effort.

items.name: Enforcing baselines
items.detail: Every system is configured the same way, every time.

items.name: Standard infrastructure configurations
items.detail: Consistent builds reduce errors and drift.

items.name: Scaling securely
items.detail: Security grows automatically with the environment.

items.name: Employee retention
items.detail: Staff spend less time on repetitive tasks.

items.name: Reaction time
items.detail: Machines respond to incidents in seconds.

items.name: Workforce multiplier
items.detail: A small team can do the work of a much larger one.

items.name: Drawbacks
items.detail: Complexity, cost, a single point of failure (a broken script breaks everything), technical debt, and ongoing supportability.

definition: Ensuring authorized users have reliable and timely access to information and systems when needed.
examContext: Expect availability tied to denial-of-service attacks, redundancy, and fault tolerance questions; the exam tests recognizing availability-impacting incidents.
analogy: Like a 24-hour store that must stay open and stocked whenever customers want to shop.
relatedTerms: CIA triad, Fault tolerance, High availability, Failover, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures a load-balanced, multi-region web cluster so that if one data center loses power, customer traffic automatically fails over to another region without downtime.
detail.quizQuestion: A retailer's website goes offline for six hours after a DDoS attack. No data was altered or disclosed. Which part of the CIA triad was MOST directly affected?
quizOptions: A) Availability, because authorized users could not reach the service when needed
B) Non-repudiation, because customers could deny that they had placed their orders
C) Confidentiality, because the attack exposed customer data to unauthorized parties
D) Integrity, because the attack changed the content of the orders in the database
detail.explanation: A denial of service that keeps authorized users from reaching a service is an availability failure. Nothing was disclosed or altered, so confidentiality and integrity were not affected, and non-repudiation concerns proving actions.

definition: A hidden method of bypassing normal authentication or security controls to gain unauthorized access to a system, often installed by malware or a malicious insider.
examContext: Exam tests backdoors as providing persistent remote access, sometimes intentionally left by developers for testing and forgotten, or installed as a payload by a trojan.
analogy: Like a hidden spare key an intruder leaves under the mat after their first break-in, so they can return anytime.
relatedTerms: Trojan horse, Rootkit, Persistence, Command and control

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's security audit discovers an unauthorized remote access account quietly installed on the web server months earlier, giving attackers a standing backdoor that bypassed the normal login process entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: Penetration testers find that a vendor's application contains a hidden administrator login that is not documented and bypasses normal authentication. The vendor says developers left it in for testing. Which of the following BEST describes the risk?
quizOptions: A) Anyone who discovers the backdoor gains persistent access that bypasses authentication
B) The backdoor is limited to the test environment, so production systems are unaffected
C) The backdoor is harmless because it can be used only by the vendor's developers
D) The backdoor only affects availability because it slows the application's login page
detail.explanation: A hidden login that bypasses authentication gives persistent access to whoever finds or learns of it, even if developers left it. The risk is not limited to the vendor, to a test environment, or to availability.

definition: A predefined set of steps to reverse a change and return a system to its previous working state if the change fails or causes problems. It is normally required before a change is approved.
examContext: Part of change management alongside approvals, impact analysis, testing and a maintenance window. Also called a rollback plan. A change without a backout plan is a red flag for a change advisory board.
analogy: The way back down the mountain, planned before you start climbing.
relatedTerms: Change management, Maintenance window, Standard operating procedure, Disaster recovery

detail.practicalScenario: Before upgrading the production database, the team documents the backout plan: take a snapshot, keep the old version installed and define the exact steps and time limit for rolling back if tests fail.
detail.quizQuestion: A change advisory board is reviewing a request to upgrade a database cluster on Saturday night. The request includes test results, an impact analysis and a maintenance window, but no description of how to return to the previous version if the upgrade fails. Which of the following should the board require BEFORE approving it?
quizOptions: A) A new service level agreement with the database vendor for after-hours support
B) A longer maintenance window so that the upgrade can be repeated if it fails
C) A penetration test of the upgraded cluster after the change is completed
D) A backout plan that reverses the change and restores the previous working state
detail.explanation: A backout (rollback) plan is a normally required part of change approval because it defines how to restore service if the change fails. A longer window, a post-change test and a vendor SLA do not provide a way back.

items.name: Approval process
items.detail: A formal review (often by a Change Advisory Board) before any change is made.

items.name: Ownership
items.detail: A named person responsible for the change.

items.name: Stakeholders
items.detail: Everyone affected who must be informed or consulted.

items.name: Impact analysis
items.detail: What could break, and how risky is the change?

items.name: Test results
items.detail: Proof the change works in a non-production environment first.

items.name: Backout plan
items.detail: The steps to undo the change if it fails.

items.name: Maintenance window
items.detail: A scheduled time when changes are allowed so users are least affected.

items.name: Standard operating procedure
items.detail: The documented way routine changes are performed.

definition: A copy of data or systems stored separately so it can be restored after loss, corruption, deletion or disaster. Backups are measured by how often they run (RPO), where they are stored and how long a restore takes (RTO).
examContext: Know full, incremental, differential and snapshot; onsite versus offsite; encryption; regularly testing restores; the 3-2-1 rule; and keeping at least one copy offline or immutable so ransomware cannot reach it.
analogy: A spare key kept at a friend's house.
relatedTerms: Full backup, Incremental backup, Differential backup, Snapshot, Disaster recovery, Ransomware

detail.practicalScenario: A company keeps three copies of its data: the live system, a nightly backup on local disk and an encrypted copy in another region with immutability turned on. After ransomware hits, it restores from the immutable copy.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's backups run nightly to a NAS that is mounted on the production network. Ransomware encrypts the file servers and then the NAS. Which of the following changes would BEST ensure the company can recover next time?
quizOptions: A) Compress the backups to reduce the storage space that the NAS consumes each night
B) Keep an offline or immutable copy of the backups and test restores regularly
C) Move the NAS to a faster network switch so that restores finish more quickly
D) Run the backups every hour to the same mounted NAS so that less data is lost
detail.explanation: Backups that ransomware can reach get encrypted too, so keep at least one copy offline or immutable, as in the 3-2-1 rule, and verify restores. More frequent backups to the same reachable NAS, compression and faster switches do not protect the copies.

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: A documented, approved standard set of security settings and software configurations for a system type, used as a reference point to detect unauthorized changes and ensure consistency across deployments.
examContext: Know baseline configurations are compared against current states to detect configuration drift; exam scenarios test recognizing deviation from baseline as a sign of unauthorized change or compromise.
analogy: Like a factory blueprint that every unit must match, any deviation from the blueprint signals something changed from the approved design.
relatedTerms: Hardening, Change management

detail.practicalScenario: Alex creates a baseline configuration template for all new web servers, specifying required security settings, and uses automated compliance scanning to flag any server whose running configuration has drifted from that approved baseline.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan shows that three web servers deployed from the same template six months ago now have different services enabled and different registry settings. No change requests were approved. Which of the following BEST describes the problem and how to detect it?
quizOptions: A) Privilege escalation, detected by reviewing the sudo logs on each of the web servers
B) Certificate expiration, detected by checking the validity dates on the web server certificates
C) Resource exhaustion, detected by monitoring CPU and memory use on each of the servers
D) Configuration drift, detected by comparing each server against the approved baseline
detail.explanation: Settings that diverge from the approved template without change requests are configuration drift, found by comparing the current state with the baseline. Privilege escalation, resource exhaustion and certificate expiry do not explain differing settings.

variants.title: Policy, standard, procedure and guideline compared

items.name: Policy
items.detail: A high-level management statement of WHAT must be done and why. Broad, mandatory, and rarely changed (for example the Acceptable Use Policy).

items.name: Standard
items.detail: Specific, MANDATORY requirements that support a policy (passwords of 14+ characters, AES-256 for data at rest).

items.name: Procedure
items.detail: Step-by-step instructions on HOW to carry out a task (an onboarding checklist, a restore runbook).

items.name: Guideline
items.detail: Recommended best practice. ADVISORY and flexible, not mandatory.

items.name: Baseline
items.detail: The minimum secure configuration that systems must meet (see secure baseline).

items.name: Common policies
items.detail: Acceptable use, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management, password, remote access, data retention and onboarding/offboarding.

items.name: Workstations and endpoints
items.detail: Install endpoint protection, enable a host firewall, patch, encrypt the disk, remove unnecessary software and bloatware, and run as a standard user.

items.name: Servers
items.detail: Minimal role-specific installs, disable unneeded services, patch, least privilege, logging and a secure baseline.

items.name: Switches and routers
items.detail: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH rather than Telnet, SNMPv3, port security, ACLs and firmware updates.

items.name: Cloud infrastructure
items.detail: Least-privilege IAM, MFA, no public storage buckets, encryption, logging and configuration scanning.

items.name: Mobile devices
items.detail: MDM policies, passcodes, encryption, remote wipe, app allow lists, and no sideloading.

items.name: IoT and embedded
items.detail: Change default credentials, update firmware, isolate on their own VLAN, and disable unused features.

items.name: ICS / SCADA / RTOS
items.detail: Segmentation or an air gap, strict physical security, monitoring and compensating controls, because patching is often impractical.

items.name: Common steps
items.detail: Change default passwords, disable unnecessary ports and protocols, remove unnecessary software, patch, and install endpoint protection.

definition: An authentication factor category based on something you are, using unique physical or behavioral characteristics such as fingerprints, facial geometry, iris patterns, or voice to verify identity.
examContext: Know biometrics as a something-you-are factor, and the exam-relevant metrics: false acceptance rate, false rejection rate, and the crossover error rate where they are equal, used to judge biometric system accuracy.
analogy: Like recognizing a close friend by their face and voice instantly, without needing them to show ID or state a password.
relatedTerms: Multifactor authentication, Smart card

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys fingerprint scanners at the data center entrance as a biometric access control, and during testing adjusts the sensor's sensitivity to balance the false acceptance rate against the false rejection rate for optimal security without excessive employee frustration.
detail.quizQuestion: A company evaluates two fingerprint readers. Reader A has a false acceptance rate of 0.1 percent and a false rejection rate of 5 percent. Reader B has equal rates of 1.5 percent for both. The data center is highly sensitive, and rejecting a legitimate user only causes a short delay. Which of the following is the BEST choice?
quizOptions: A) Reader A, because a low false acceptance rate matters most for a sensitive area
B) Reader B, because its crossover error rate makes it the more secure device in every case
C) Reader B, because equal error rates mean that unauthorized users are never accepted
D) Reader A, because a low false rejection rate matters most for a sensitive area
detail.explanation: A false acceptance lets an unauthorized person in, so a sensitive area favors the reader with the lowest FAR even if it rejects more legitimate users. A lower crossover error rate is a general accuracy measure and is not the deciding factor here, and Reader A's FRR is actually the high one.

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: Fingerprint
items.detail: Cheap and widely accepted, but can be fooled by lifted prints or fakes unless liveness detection is used.

items.name: Retina
items.detail: Scans the blood-vessel pattern at the back of the eye. Very accurate but intrusive, so uncommon.

items.name: Iris
items.detail: Scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Accurate and stable over a lifetime, and less intrusive than retina.

items.name: Facial recognition
items.detail: Convenient, but affected by lighting and angle, and spoofable with photos or masks without liveness checks.

items.name: Voice
items.detail: Affected by noise and illness; spoofable with recordings or deepfakes.

items.name: Vein / palm
items.detail: Maps the pattern of blood vessels; difficult to forge.

items.name: Gait
items.detail: A behavioral biometric based on how a person walks.

items.name: FRR (Type I)
items.detail: False Rejection Rate: a LEGITIMATE user is wrongly denied. Hurts usability.

items.name: FAR (Type II)
items.detail: False Acceptance Rate: an IMPOSTOR is wrongly allowed in. This is the dangerous one for security.

items.name: CER / EER
items.detail: Crossover (Equal) Error Rate: the point where FAR equals FRR. The LOWER the CER, the more accurate the system.

definition: A type of collision attack that exploits the mathematics of probability, which shows that finding two inputs sharing the same hash output requires far fewer attempts than brute-forcing one specific hash, named for the statistical surprise behind the birthday paradox.
examContext: Know the birthday attack as the probability-based reasoning behind why collision attacks against hash functions succeed faster than brute-force intuition would suggest, which is why hash digests need sufficient output length to resist them.
analogy: Like discovering it only takes about 23 random people in a room before two likely share the same birthday, far fewer than the 366 you'd assume are needed, because you're comparing everyone against everyone, not just against one fixed date.
relatedTerms: Collision attack, Hashing, Key stretching

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan explains to the development team why the new hashing scheme needs a long output length: a birthday attack means an attacker needs far fewer guesses than the total possible hash values to find two inputs that collide, so a short digest would be crackable much sooner than it looks.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst explains why a hash function with a short 64-bit output is risky for digital signatures: an attacker can find two different documents with the same hash in roughly four billion attempts instead of about eighteen quintillion. Which of the following attacks does this describe?
quizOptions: A) A replay attack, which resubmits a captured message to trick the receiving system
B) A downgrade attack, which forces a connection to use a weaker version of a protocol
C) A rainbow table attack, which uses precomputed hash chains to reverse password hashes
D) A birthday attack, which uses probability to find hash collisions faster than brute force
detail.explanation: Finding any two inputs with the same hash takes far fewer attempts than matching one specific hash, which is the birthday attack and the reason digests need enough bits. Rainbow tables reverse hashes, downgrade attacks weaken protocols, and replay attacks resend messages.

definition: Unwanted software pre-installed by a device manufacturer or bundled with other programs. It wastes resources, may contain vulnerabilities or telemetry, and increases the attack surface.
examContext: Handled during hardening by removing unnecessary software. Related terms: PUP (potentially unwanted program) and adware.
analogy: The promotional flyers a car dealer leaves in the glove box: you did not ask for them, and they only take up space.
relatedTerms: Hardening, Attack surface, Adware, PUP, Secure baseline

detail.practicalScenario: A new laptop arrives with a dozen trial programs and a manufacturer utility that has a known vulnerability. IT's standard image removes all of them before deployment to shrink the attack surface.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's new laptops arrive with trial software, manufacturer utilities and third-party toolbars that the company does not need. Some of the utilities run background services with known vulnerabilities. Which of the following is the BEST way to address this during deployment?
quizOptions: A) Install a second antivirus product to protect the pre-installed software on every laptop
B) Leave the software in place but block its network access with the host firewall
C) Let users decide which pre-installed programs to remove once they start using the laptops
D) Build a hardened image that removes the unnecessary software before deployment
detail.explanation: Removing unnecessary software in a hardened baseline image shrinks the attack surface before devices reach users. Leaving it to users is inconsistent, a second antivirus does not fix vulnerabilities, and firewalling leaves vulnerable code installed.

definition: A symmetric encryption algorithm that encrypts data in fixed-size chunks, such as AES's 128-bit blocks, often requiring padding and an operation mode like CBC or GCM for data that doesn't fit evenly.
examContext: Know AES as the standard block cipher; the exam may ask you to distinguish block ciphers, which use fixed-size chunks, from stream ciphers, which process data continuously bit by bit.
analogy: Like washing dishes in fixed-size batches in a dishwasher, rather than one plate at a time.
relatedTerms: Stream cipher, Symmetric encryption, Cipher suite

detail.practicalScenario: Sam selects AES-256 in GCM mode to encrypt stored customer records, taking advantage of the block cipher's fixed-size block processing plus built-in authentication to detect any tampering with the encrypted data.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineer must encrypt a 40-byte message with AES, which works on 16-byte blocks. Which of the following BEST describes what the encryption process needs in order to handle the message?
quizOptions: A) A public and private key pair, because AES encrypts each block with one key pair
B) A stream of random bits that is XORed with the message one bit at a time
C) A mode of operation such as CBC or GCM, with padding where the mode requires it
D) A hash of the message, because AES cannot process data that is not a multiple of 16
detail.explanation: AES is a block cipher, so longer messages need a mode of operation such as CBC or GCM, and modes like CBC also need padding for a partial final block. Bit-by-bit XOR describes stream ciphers, AES is symmetric rather than key-pair based, and hashing is not part of the process.

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: A distributed, append-only ledger technology in which transactions are grouped into cryptographically linked blocks and validated by a decentralized consensus mechanism, making records resistant to unauthorized alteration without a central authority.
examContext: Know blockchain is presented as a cryptographic solution that provides integrity and non-repudiation for a shared transaction history through decentralized consensus, rather than a tool for confidentiality.
analogy: Like a shared ledger book copied identically across hundreds of accountants' desks; to fake one entry, you'd have to secretly change every single copy at once, which is practically impossible.
relatedTerms: Hashing, Digital signature, Non-repudiation, Integrity, Encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's supply chain team implements a blockchain-based ledger to record each time a shipment changes custody between manufacturers, carriers, and warehouses, so that every party can verify the shipment's full history has not been tampered with, without needing to trust a single central database owner.
detail.quizQuestion: Several competing companies want a shared record of shipments that none of them can alter in secret and that no single party controls. Which of the following BEST describes the property that blockchain provides for this purpose?
quizOptions: A) Anonymity of the participants, because the ledger never links an action to a key
B) Confidentiality of every transaction, because the blocks are encrypted with a shared key
C) Availability of the ledger, because a central server holds a mirrored copy of each block
D) Integrity of a shared history, through cryptographically linked blocks and consensus
detail.explanation: A blockchain gives integrity and non-repudiation for a shared history by linking blocks with hashes and validating them through decentralized consensus. It is not primarily a confidentiality tool, it has no central server, and actions are tied to keys.

definition: The internal or hired group of defenders responsible for monitoring, detecting, and responding to security threats and attacks, including those simulated by a red team during an exercise.
examContext: Know the blue team consists of defenders who use SIEM, IDS/IPS, and monitoring tools to detect and respond to attacks; often contrasted with the red team on the exam.
analogy: Like the home security guards and response crew who must detect and stop the simulated intruders during a training drill.
relatedTerms: Red team, Purple team, Threat hunting

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's blue team monitors SIEM alerts throughout the red team engagement, successfully detecting the simulated attacker's lateral movement attempt within twenty minutes and isolating the affected workstation before further compromise.
detail.quizQuestion: During a security exercise, one group monitors the SIEM, investigates alerts and tries to detect and stop simulated attacks launched by another group. Which of the following BEST describes the first group?
quizOptions: A) The red team, which simulates real attacks to test how well the organization's defenses work
B) The white team, which sets the rules of the exercise and referees its outcome
C) The blue team, which defends the organization by monitoring, detecting and responding
D) The purple team, which helps attackers and defenders share what they learn
detail.explanation: The blue team defends: it monitors, detects and responds to attacks. The red team attacks, the purple team promotes collaboration and knowledge sharing between them, and the white team governs the exercise.

items.name: Red team
items.detail: OFFENSE: simulates real attackers to find weaknesses.

items.name: Blue team
items.detail: DEFENSE: monitors, detects and responds to attacks, and hardens systems.

items.name: Purple team
items.detail: Red and blue working together and sharing findings in real time to improve detection and response.

items.name: White team
items.detail: Referees and sets the rules of an exercise (scope, scoring, safety).

definition: Sending unsolicited messages or contact cards to nearby Bluetooth-enabled devices. It is more of an annoyance and does not steal data.
examContext: Contrast with bluesnarfing, which steals data. Mitigation: set Bluetooth to non-discoverable or turn it off when not in use.
analogy: Dropping unwanted flyers under windshield wipers in a parking lot.
relatedTerms: Bluesnarfing, BLE, Evil twin, War driving

detail.practicalScenario: A commuter's phone shows a spam message from an unknown nearby Bluetooth device. Nothing is copied from the phone; the sender only wanted to push a message.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees at a conference report receiving unsolicited messages with a contact card on their phones from an unknown nearby device. No data appears to have been taken. Which of the following BEST describes this activity and the simplest preventive step?
quizOptions: A) Bluejacking, prevented by setting Bluetooth to non-discoverable or turning it off
B) Evil twin, prevented by hiding the SSID on the access points near the conference
C) War driving, prevented by turning off the broadcast beacon on the access points
D) Bluesnarfing, prevented by setting Bluetooth to non-discoverable or turning it off
detail.explanation: Unsolicited messages or contact cards sent to nearby Bluetooth devices, with no data theft, are bluejacking, and non-discoverable mode or turning Bluetooth off prevents it. Bluesnarfing steals data, and evil twin and war driving are Wi-Fi attacks.

definition: Unauthorized access to a Bluetooth device to steal data such as contacts, calendar entries and messages, exploiting vulnerable pairing or protocol flaws.
examContext: More serious than bluejacking. Defenses: turn off Bluetooth when not in use, disable discoverable mode, patch firmware and require pairing approval.
analogy: A pickpocket quietly lifting your wallet in a crowd, compared with a prankster handing you a flyer.
relatedTerms: Bluejacking, BLE, Wireless jamming, Smishing

detail.practicalScenario: In a crowded cafe, an attacker connects to an unpatched phone over Bluetooth and copies its contact list without the owner noticing. The owner later finds the data in a phishing campaign.
detail.quizQuestion: A security researcher walks through a lobby and silently extracts contacts and calendar entries from an unpatched phone that has Bluetooth enabled and discoverable. Which of the following BEST describes this attack?
quizOptions: A) Smishing, which delivers phishing links to the phone through text messages
B) Bluejacking, which sends unsolicited messages or contact cards to nearby Bluetooth devices
C) Bluesnarfing, which steals data over Bluetooth by exploiting pairing or protocol flaws
D) Jamming, which floods the radio frequency band to disrupt wireless service
detail.explanation: Extracting data from a Bluetooth device without authorization is bluesnarfing. Bluejacking only sends unsolicited messages, smishing uses text messages, and jamming disrupts the radio signal rather than stealing data.

definition: A short, sturdy vertical post installed in the ground, typically in a row, to block vehicle access to a pedestrian area or building entrance while still allowing people to walk through.
examContext: An objective 1.2 physical security control; the exam tests recognizing bollards as a vehicle-specific barrier, distinct from fencing, which blocks both people and vehicles along a full perimeter.
analogy: Like a row of concrete teeth planted outside a storefront that stop a car from driving in but let shoppers walk right past.
relatedTerms: Fencing, Access control vestibule, Security guard

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's facilities team installs a line of steel bollards along the sidewalk in front of the data center's main entrance to prevent a vehicle-ramming attack while keeping the walkway open for employees on foot.
detail.quizQuestion: A retailer's glass entrance faces a parking lot. After a vehicle crashed through the doors, the owner wants to stop vehicles from reaching the entrance while still letting shoppers walk up to the doors. Which of the following controls BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) An access control vestibule installed just inside the main entrance doors
B) Security cameras that are mounted above the entrance doors and aimed at the lot
C) A tall perimeter fence installed around the whole parking lot and the entrance
D) A row of bollards installed along the front of the building near the entrance
detail.explanation: Bollards are sturdy posts that block vehicles while allowing pedestrians through. A full fence blocks shoppers too, a vestibule controls how people enter rather than stopping vehicles, and cameras only detect.

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

definition: A network of compromised, internet-connected devices known as bots that are remotely controlled by an attacker, typically used to carry out coordinated attacks such as distributed denial of service.
examContext: Exam tests botnets as directed through command-and-control infrastructure, commonly used for DDoS attacks, spam, or large-scale cryptomining.
analogy: Like a puppet master pulling the strings on thousands of zombie puppets all at once.
relatedTerms: Command and control, Malware, Cryptojacking

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's network team notices thousands of compromised IoT cameras worldwide suddenly flooding a company's web server with traffic simultaneously, all controlled remotely as part of a coordinated botnet.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's web servers are overwhelmed by traffic from 40,000 IP addresses that belong to home routers and cameras around the world. Investigators find that the devices contact a small number of servers every few minutes for instructions. Which of the following BEST describes the infrastructure behind the attack?
quizOptions: A) A peer-to-peer network in which volunteers share files directly with one another
B) A botnet of compromised devices that take orders from command-and-control servers
C) A reflection attack in which innocent public servers send responses to the victim
D) A watering hole attack in which a popular website delivers malware to its visitors
detail.explanation: Thousands of compromised devices that check in with a few servers for instructions are a botnet controlled through command and control. A reflection attack uses uninvolved servers rather than check-ins, a watering hole delivers malware to visitors, and P2P networks are voluntary.

definition: An attack in which the attacker mimics a well-known company's logos, branding, email templates, or overall look and feel to deceive victims into trusting a fraudulent message, website, or call.
examContext: The exam treats brand impersonation as a broader deception tactic that can combine with phishing, typosquatting, or vishing; the key detail is that the attack relies on borrowed visual or verbal trust rather than any single technical method.
analogy: Like a counterfeiter printing a fake designer label onto a cheap bag, relying on the recognizable brand to earn instant trust it hasn't actually earned.
relatedTerms: Typosquatting, Phishing, Vishing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team flags a phishing campaign that perfectly replicates a major bank's logo, email formatting, and color scheme in a message warning customers their account is locked, convincing many recipients the email is legitimate.
detail.quizQuestion: Customers receive emails and text messages that copy a bank's logo, colors and email template and link to a convincing replica of its login page. Which of the following BEST describes the technique that makes the messages believable?
quizOptions: A) Brand impersonation, which borrows a trusted company's visual identity to earn trust
B) Watering hole, which compromises a site that the targeted group visits often
C) Whaling, which targets senior executives with highly personalized messages
D) Pharming, which silently redirects a correctly typed address to a fraudulent server
detail.explanation: Copying a company's logos, templates and look and feel to borrow its trust is brand impersonation, often combined with phishing. Pharming redirects traffic through DNS, a watering hole compromises a site visited by the target, and whaling targets executives.

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: The group of devices that receive each other's broadcast frames, in other words all devices on the same Layer 2 network. Switches forward broadcasts to every port in a VLAN, while routers do not forward them, so each VLAN and each router interface is its own broadcast domain.
examContext: Routers and VLANs split broadcast domains, while hubs and plain switches do not. Smaller broadcast domains mean less noise and a smaller area for attacks that rely on broadcasts, such as ARP poisoning and rogue DHCP servers.
analogy: Everyone within earshot of a loudspeaker announcement; walls keep it from reaching other rooms.
relatedTerms: VLAN, Switch, Router, Collision domain, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: A flat office network of 400 devices suffers from heavy broadcast traffic. The team splits it into four VLANs, and each VLAN becomes its own, smaller broadcast domain.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's flat network of 600 hosts experiences heavy broadcast traffic, and a recent ARP poisoning incident affected every host. The team wants to reduce the area that broadcast-based attacks can reach without buying new switches. Which of the following BEST accomplishes this?
quizOptions: A) Enable port mirroring on every access port so that the broadcasts are copied
B) Increase the ARP cache timeout on each host so that fewer broadcasts are sent
C) Segment the network into VLANs so that each VLAN has a smaller broadcast domain
D) Replace the switches with hubs so that every port shares one collision domain
detail.explanation: VLANs and routers split broadcast domains, so broadcast-based attacks such as ARP poisoning reach fewer hosts and there is less noise. Hubs enlarge the shared domain, mirroring only copies traffic, and a longer ARP cache timeout does not limit the reach of an attack.

definition: An attack method that systematically attempts every possible combination of characters or keys until the correct password or cryptographic key is found, requiring significant computational time but guaranteed to eventually succeed against an unlimited attempt budget.
examContext: Know brute force differs from dictionary attacks, which try a curated wordlist instead of every combination; mitigations include account lockout, key stretching, and strong, long passwords; the exam may ask you to identify this versus other password attacks from a description.
analogy: Like trying every single number combination on a padlock one by one until it finally opens.
relatedTerms: Account lockout, Key stretching, Dictionary attack, Credential stuffing

detail.practicalScenario: Alex notices in the authentication logs that a single account received tens of thousands of login attempts using sequentially generated password strings within an hour, and recognizes this systematic character-by-character approach as a brute force attack rather than a targeted guess.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst reviewing logs sees 80,000 login attempts against one account in an hour, trying passwords such as aaaaaa, aaaaab and aaaaac in sequence. Which of the following attack types BEST matches this pattern?
quizOptions: A) Password spraying, which tries one common password against many different accounts
B) Brute force, which systematically tries every possible combination of characters
C) Dictionary, which tries words and phrases from a curated list of likely passwords
D) Credential stuffing, which tries username and password pairs from other breaches
detail.explanation: Sequential attempts through all combinations are brute force. A dictionary attack uses a wordlist, spraying uses a few passwords across many accounts, and credential stuffing reuses breached pairs.

items.name: Length
items.detail: The strongest single factor against guessing and cracking. Favor long passphrases over short complex strings.

items.name: Complexity
items.detail: Requires mixed character types. Current NIST guidance prefers length plus a blocklist of known-bad passwords over forced complexity.

items.name: Reuse / history
items.detail: Password history stops users from recycling their last N passwords.

items.name: Expiration / maximum age
items.detail: Forces a change after a set time. Current NIST guidance says do not force routine changes unless there is evidence of compromise.

items.name: Minimum age
items.detail: Stops a user from changing the password repeatedly in one sitting to cycle back to an old one.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Locks the account after N failed attempts. Defeats online brute force, but can be abused to lock out legitimate users (a denial of service).

items.name: Password manager
items.detail: Generates and stores unique strong passwords so users do not reuse them. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

items.name: Passwordless
items.detail: FIDO2 keys, passkeys and biometrics remove the shared secret that attackers phish or crack.

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: A software vulnerability that occurs when a program writes more data to a memory buffer than it was allocated to hold, potentially overwriting adjacent memory and allowing code execution.
examContext: Exam tests buffer overflow as a classic application vulnerability, mitigated through input validation, bounds checking, and secure coding practices such as data execution prevention and address space layout randomization.
analogy: Like overfilling a glass of water until it spills onto and damages the papers sitting next to it on the table.
relatedTerms: Exploit, Vulnerability, Privilege escalation

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's code review tool flags a function that fails to validate input length before copying it into a fixed-size array, a classic buffer overflow flaw that could let an attacker overwrite memory and execute arbitrary code.
detail.quizQuestion: A tester sends a 5,000-character string to a field that the application stores in a 256-byte memory buffer. The application crashes, and a debugger shows that the tester's data overwrote the return address on the stack. Which of the following mitigations would BEST prevent this vulnerability at the source?
quizOptions: A) Validate input length and use bounds checking in the code that copies data
B) Require multifactor authentication for every user who submits data to the field
C) Encrypt the data with TLS while it travels between the client and the server
D) Increase the size of the database that stores the values the application receives
detail.explanation: Overflows happen when code copies more data than a buffer can hold, so validating input length and checking bounds in the code prevents it, with DEP and ASLR as extra layers. TLS, MFA and database size do not change how the buffer is handled.

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: A program that rewards independent researchers with money or recognition for responsibly reporting valid security vulnerabilities in an organization's systems, within defined scope and rules.
examContext: A vulnerability identification method alongside responsible disclosure programs, often run through platforms such as HackerOne or Bugcrowd. It defines scope, safe harbor and payouts.
analogy: A reward poster for anyone who finds and reports a hole in the fence.
relatedTerms: Responsible disclosure, Penetration testing, Vulnerability, Rules of engagement

detail.practicalScenario: A software company publishes a bounty policy listing which systems are in scope and what each severity pays. A researcher reports a serious flaw privately, the company fixes it and pays the reward.
detail.quizQuestion: A software company wants independent researchers to find vulnerabilities in its web applications and report them privately, in return for cash rewards. It wants to define which systems are in scope and offer legal safe harbor to participants. Which of the following BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) An internal audit, in which the company's own staff review its controls against a standard
B) A bug bounty program, which pays researchers for responsibly reported valid vulnerabilities
C) A penetration test, in which a hired team attacks the systems within an agreed scope
D) A honeypot deployment, in which decoy systems attract attackers so that they can be studied
detail.explanation: A bug bounty program rewards independent researchers for responsibly reporting valid vulnerabilities within a defined scope and safe harbor. A penetration test is a contracted engagement, an internal audit uses the company's staff, and a honeypot lures attackers.

definition: The planning and preparation that ensures an organization's critical business functions can continue operating during and after a disruptive event, encompassing policies, procedures, and resources beyond just IT systems.
examContext: Know business continuity planning is broader than disaster recovery, since it covers the whole organization's ability to keep operating including people, processes, and facilities, while disaster recovery focuses specifically on restoring IT systems; know the business impact analysis as a key supporting activity.
analogy: Like a company having a backup plan to keep serving customers from a temporary location with pen-and-paper processes even if the main office and all computers are completely unavailable.
relatedTerms: Disaster recovery, Fault tolerance, High availability

detail.practicalScenario: Sam leads a business continuity planning exercise that identifies critical functions like order processing and customer support, then establishes manual fallback procedures and an alternate work site so the company can keep serving customers even if the main office becomes unusable.
detail.quizQuestion: After a flood closes a company's headquarters, the IT team restores the servers at a recovery site, but the company cannot resume operations because employees have no workspace, the call center has no phones and key suppliers were never notified. Which of the following BEST describes what was missing?
quizOptions: A) Business continuity planning that covers people, processes and facilities beyond IT
B) A vulnerability management program that tracks and patches all of the company's systems
C) A security awareness program that teaches employees to recognize phishing emails
D) A disaster recovery plan that restores the servers and the data at an alternate site
detail.explanation: Business continuity is broader than IT recovery: it covers people, processes, facilities and suppliers so that critical functions continue. The IT recovery in the scenario worked, so disaster recovery was not the gap, and patching and awareness programs are unrelated.

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: A targeted social engineering attack in which an attacker compromises or convincingly spoofs a trusted email account, often an executive's, to trick an employee into wiring money, changing payment details, or disclosing sensitive information.
examContext: The exam frequently pairs BEC with whaling and invoice-fraud scenarios; a key detail is that BEC often requires no malware at all, relying purely on a convincing, well-researched impersonation of a trusted sender.
analogy: Like a con artist forging a signature on a company check, imitating the boss's handwriting well enough that the bank teller doesn't question it.
relatedTerms: Whaling, Phishing, Spear phishing, Social engineering, Pretexting

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's finance department receives an urgent email appearing to come from the CFO's exact email address requesting an immediate wire transfer to a new vendor account, which the team catches only after calling the CFO directly to verify.
detail.quizQuestion: An accounts payable clerk receives an email that appears to come from the CFO, using the CFO's real name and a lookalike address, asking for an urgent wire transfer to a new vendor account. The email contains no attachments or links. Which of the following controls would BEST help prevent this attack from succeeding?
quizOptions: A) A sandbox that detonates email attachments before they reach the user's inbox for review
B) A web filter that blocks employees from visiting newly registered domains
C) An endpoint antivirus product that scans the clerk's workstation each night
D) A process requiring out-of-band verification and dual approval for payment changes
detail.explanation: BEC relies on impersonation with no malware, so technical filters miss it, while procedural controls such as callback verification and dual approval for payment changes stop the fraud. A sandbox needs attachments, web filtering needs links, and antivirus finds malware.
