definition: A method of testing an application for security vulnerabilities by executing it and observing its actual behavior, inputs, and outputs while it runs, rather than examining its source code.
examContext: Know dynamic analysis tests the running application itself, often able to catch runtime issues like session-handling flaws that a static review of source code alone would miss; the two techniques are complementary, not competing.
analogy: Like taste-testing the dish while it's actually cooking on the stove, rather than just reading over the recipe beforehand.
relatedTerms: Static code analysis, Sandboxing, Penetration testing

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's QA team runs the web application in a staging environment and feeds it a barrage of malformed and unexpected inputs while monitoring its live responses, catching a session-handling flaw that only appears while the application is actually executing, something the earlier static source code scan never flagged.
detail.quizQuestion: A team scanned its source code with a static analysis tool and found no issues, but an assessment of the running application found a session-handling flaw that lets one user hijack another user's session. Which testing method would MOST likely have found this flaw earlier?
quizOptions: A) Code signing, which verifies the integrity of the compiled application before release
B) Dynamic analysis, which tests the running application and observes how it behaves
C) A software bill of materials, which lists the third-party components in the application
D) Static analysis, which examines the source code again without running the program
detail.explanation: Dynamic analysis executes the application and observes inputs, outputs and session behavior, so it finds runtime flaws that source review misses. Static analysis was already run, code signing verifies integrity, and an SBOM lists components.

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: The process of identifying, collecting, preserving, and producing electronically stored information (ESI) in response to litigation, regulatory inquiries, or investigations.
examContext: Know e-Discovery is the process of identifying, collecting, and producing electronically stored information for litigation or investigation, and that it typically follows a legal hold.
analogy: Like a librarian tasked with finding every book, note, and sticky tab in a massive archive that mentions a specific topic, then handing a complete, organized copy to the lawyers.
relatedTerms: Legal hold, Chain of custody, Data classification, Incident response

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's team uses specialized e-Discovery software to search across years of archived emails and file shares for every message mentioning a specific contract dispute, then exports the results with metadata intact so outside counsel can review them for an upcoming lawsuit.
detail.quizQuestion: A company receives notice of a lawsuit and must produce relevant emails and documents. The legal team tells IT to stop the automatic deletion of mailboxes for the employees involved, and then to locate, collect and deliver the relevant electronic records to opposing counsel. Which of the following pairs BEST identifies these two activities?
quizOptions: A) A legal hold to preserve the records, followed by e-discovery to collect and produce them
B) A chain of custody log of the records, followed by a retention schedule that deletes them
C) E-discovery to collect the records, followed by a legal hold after they are produced
D) A legal hold to preserve the records, followed by sanitization to remove duplicate copies
detail.explanation: A legal hold suspends normal deletion to preserve relevant data, and e-discovery then identifies, collects and produces the electronically stored information. The hold comes first, sanitizing or deleting records would destroy evidence, and a chain of custody log documents handling rather than preserving.

variants.title: Digital forensics: order of volatility and handling

items.name: Order of volatility
items.detail: Collect the MOST volatile evidence first: CPU registers and cache, then RAM (routing/ARP tables, processes), then swap/page file, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.

items.name: Preservation
items.detail: Use write blockers, work on forensic copies, and hash the image to prove it was not changed.

items.name: Acquisition
items.detail: A bit-for-bit disk image, a memory dump, or a snapshot. Live acquisition is needed to capture volatile data.

items.name: Chain of custody
items.detail: Documented record of who handled the evidence, when and why. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible.

items.name: Legal hold
items.detail: A mandate to preserve relevant data (stop normal deletion) because of litigation or investigation.

items.name: e-Discovery
items.detail: Identifying and collecting electronic information for legal proceedings.

items.name: Timeline and reporting
items.detail: Reconstruct events, document findings and make the report clear and reproducible.

definition: A computer system with a dedicated function built into a larger device, such as a printer, smart TV, medical device or vehicle controller, usually running fixed firmware with limited resources.
examContext: Security challenges: inability to patch, weak defaults, long lifespans and too little compute for security agents. Defenses: segmentation, compensating controls and monitoring.
analogy: The tiny computer in a microwave: it does one job and nobody expects to update it.
relatedTerms: RTOS, IoT, ICS, SCADA, Compensating control, Hardening

detail.practicalScenario: A hospital's infusion pumps run old embedded firmware that the vendor no longer updates. The team places them on an isolated VLAN with strict firewall rules because they cannot be patched.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital's infusion pumps run fixed firmware that the hospital cannot patch, have very limited memory, and use a default administrator password that the vendor will not let customers change. Which of the following is the BEST approach to protect them?
quizOptions: A) Add the pumps to the domain so that they receive the same group policy as laptops
B) Replace the pump firmware with the latest open-source operating system
C) Place the pumps on an isolated VLAN with restricted access and monitor the traffic
D) Install an endpoint agent on each pump to scan its memory for malware
detail.explanation: Embedded devices often cannot be patched or run agents, so compensating controls such as segmentation, restricted access and monitoring are the usual defense. Agents need resources the devices lack, replacing firmware is generally not permitted, and such devices cannot join a domain.

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: The process of wrapping data in a header (and sometimes a trailer) at each layer as it moves down the stack: data becomes a segment, then a packet, then a frame, then bits. The receiver reverses the process, which is called de-encapsulation.
examContext: Know the data unit names (data, segment, packet, frame, bits) and what each layer adds: ports at Layer 4, IP addresses at Layer 3 and MAC addresses at Layer 2. Tunneling and VPNs also encapsulate packets inside other packets.
analogy: Putting a letter in an envelope, the envelope in a shipping box and the box on a truck: each wrapper adds its own label.
relatedTerms: OSI, TCP, IP, VPN, IPSec

detail.practicalScenario: When a laptop sends a web request, the application data gets a TCP header (a segment), then an IP header (a packet), then an Ethernet header and trailer (a frame) before it is sent as signals.
detail.quizQuestion: A packet analyzer displays a frame containing an IP packet, which contains a TCP segment, which contains application data. Which of the following BEST describes the order in which headers are added as the data is prepared for transmission?
quizOptions: A) Transport (TCP) header, then data link (Ethernet) header, then network (IP) header and trailer
B) Data link (Ethernet) header, then network (IP) header, then transport (TCP) header
C) Network (IP) header, then transport (TCP) header, then data link (Ethernet) header and trailer
D) Transport (TCP) header, then network (IP) header, then data link (Ethernet) header and trailer
detail.explanation: Data moving down the stack gets a transport header (a segment), then a network header (a packet), then a data link header and trailer (a frame). The other sequences place the layers in the wrong order.

definition: The process of converting plaintext data into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and key, so that only authorized parties with the correct key can convert it back to its original form.
examContext: SY0-701 Domain 1.4 expects you to know encryption as the core mechanism for protecting data at rest, in transit, and in use; be ready to distinguish it from hashing, which is one-way and not reversible.
analogy: Like sealing a letter in a locked box that only the intended recipient has the key to open.
relatedTerms: Symmetric encryption, Asymmetric encryption, Hashing, Hybrid encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures full-disk encryption on all company laptops so that if a device is lost or stolen, the data on it remains unreadable without the recovery key, satisfying the organization's data-at-rest protection policy.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to protect customer files so that someone who steals the storage media cannot read them, but authorized staff must be able to recover the original content. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) Hashing, which converts data into a fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed
B) Encryption, which turns plaintext into ciphertext that the correct key can reverse
C) Steganography, which hides the data inside another file such as a picture or video
D) Obfuscation, which makes data harder to read but needs no key to be understood
detail.explanation: Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext that only the correct key can reverse, which protects the stored files and allows recovery. Hashing is one-way, obfuscation relies on obscurity rather than a key, and steganography hides data rather than protecting it.

items.name: Symmetric
items.detail: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts. Very fast, so it does the bulk data encryption. Weakness: securely sharing the key. N users need N(N-1)/2 keys.

items.name: Asymmetric
items.detail: A mathematically linked public/private key pair. Slow, so it is used for key exchange, digital signatures and certificates. Solves key distribution. N users need only 2N keys.

items.name: Hybrid
items.detail: Asymmetric crypto securely exchanges a random symmetric session key, then symmetric crypto encrypts the actual data. This is how TLS and most real systems work.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: No key (unless it is an HMAC) and no way back: a one-way function giving a fixed-length digest. Used for integrity and password storage, not for confidentiality.

items.name: Full-disk
items.detail: Everything on the drive, including the OS (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS). Protects a lost or stolen device; data is exposed once the system is unlocked and running.

items.name: Partition / volume
items.detail: One partition or logical volume is encrypted while others stay in the clear.

items.name: File / folder
items.detail: Individual files (EFS, GPG, 7-Zip AES). Protects specific data even from other users of the same machine.

items.name: Database
items.detail: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) encrypts the database files; column- or record-level encryption protects individual fields such as SSNs.

items.name: Transport / communication
items.detail: Protects data in motion: TLS, IPsec, SSH, WPA3. The data is not necessarily encrypted at the other end.

variants.title: Data states and how to protect each

items.name: At rest
items.detail: Stored on disk, in a database, on backups or removable media. Protect with full-disk, file or database encryption, access controls and secure storage.

items.name: In transit (in motion)
items.detail: Moving across a network. Protect with TLS, IPsec, VPN, SSH and WPA3.

items.name: In use
items.detail: Being processed in memory or by the CPU. The hardest state to protect: secure enclaves, memory encryption, access controls, and locking screens.

items.name: General methods
items.detail: Encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation, permission restrictions and geographic restrictions (geofencing).

definition: Short-lived credentials, tokens or certificates created on demand for a single task or session that expire automatically, so there is no long-term secret for attackers to steal.
examContext: Used in PAM, cloud IAM and DevOps; they reduce the window of exposure and the reliance on static secrets.
analogy: A one-day visitor badge that stops working at closing time.
relatedTerms: Just-in-time access, Password vaulting, PAM, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: A deployment pipeline requests a temporary cloud credential that is valid for 15 minutes. If the credential leaks in a log file, it is already useless by the time anyone could abuse it.
detail.quizQuestion: A DevOps pipeline currently uses a long-lived cloud access key stored in a configuration file. The security team wants the pipeline to receive a credential only when a job runs, valid for minutes, so that a stolen credential is nearly useless. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) A shared service account whose password is rotated manually once each year
B) Ephemeral credentials issued on demand that expire automatically after the job
C) Multifactor authentication on the repository where the configuration file is stored
D) A longer, more complex access key that is stored in an encrypted configuration file
detail.explanation: Ephemeral credentials are created on demand and expire automatically, leaving no long-term secret to steal. Annual rotation and longer keys still leave a standing secret, and MFA on the repository does not remove the stored key.

definition: The incident response phase in which the root cause is removed from the environment: deleting malware, closing exploited vulnerabilities, rebuilding compromised systems and resetting credentials.
examContext: Comes after containment and before recovery. If the root cause is not removed, the attacker or malware can return.
analogy: Removing every trace of the infestation, not just the visible bugs.
relatedTerms: Containment, Incident response, Lessons learned, Persistence

detail.practicalScenario: With the spread contained, the team removes the malware, patches the exploited vulnerability, rebuilds the affected servers from clean images and resets all passwords that may have been exposed.
detail.quizQuestion: An incident response team has isolated an infected server. Analysis shows that the attackers entered through an unpatched web application and created a backdoor account. Which of the following actions is part of eradication?
quizOptions: A) Patching the application, removing the backdoor account and rebuilding the server
B) Restoring the production data to the rebuilt server and then monitoring it closely
C) Documenting the timeline of events and holding a review meeting with the whole team
D) Disconnecting the server from the network to stop the malware from spreading further
detail.explanation: Eradication removes the root cause: fixing the exploited vulnerability, deleting persistence and rebuilding compromised systems. Isolation is containment, restoring data and monitoring is recovery, and the review meeting is lessons learned.

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: A rogue wireless access point configured with the same SSID as a legitimate network so victims connect to it, letting the attacker eavesdrop, capture credentials or launch on-path attacks.
examContext: Different from a generic rogue AP, which is any unauthorized AP. Defenses: WPA3 or 802.1X with certificate validation, WIDS/WIPS, a VPN on public Wi-Fi and user awareness.
analogy: A fake ATM placed next to the real one that looks identical but records your PIN.
relatedTerms: Rogue access point, Man-in-the-middle attack, Deauthentication attack, WIDS

detail.practicalScenario: At an airport, an attacker creates a network named "Airport_Free_WiFi", identical to the real one. Travelers connect to the stronger signal and the attacker captures their unencrypted traffic and login pages.
detail.quizQuestion: Travelers at an airport connect to a Wi-Fi network named like the airline's lounge network. A security analyst discovers that the network is run from an attacker's laptop and presents a portal that captures email passwords. Which of the following BEST protects users from this attack?
quizOptions: A) Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi and networks that authenticate with validated certificates
B) Joining whichever network has the strongest signal, since it is probably the real one
C) Using WEP on the legitimate network so that traffic is encrypted over the air
D) Hiding the SSID of the legitimate network so that attackers cannot copy its name
detail.explanation: An evil twin copies a legitimate SSID, so users should not trust the name alone: validating the network with certificate-based authentication such as 802.1X and tunneling traffic over a VPN protect them. Hiding the SSID, WEP and signal strength do not prove that a network is real.

definition: The unauthorized transfer or theft of data from a system or network to a location controlled by an attacker.
examContext: Exam tests exfiltration as typically the final goal in a data breach, often detected through data loss prevention tools monitoring for unusual outbound data transfers.
analogy: Like a spy smuggling stolen documents out of a building in a hidden briefcase.
relatedTerms: Command and control, Data loss prevention, Advanced persistent threat, Steganography

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's data loss prevention system alerts on an unusually large encrypted file being uploaded to a personal cloud storage account late at night, which investigation confirms was an attacker exfiltrating stolen customer records.
detail.quizQuestion: A DLP system alerts that a workstation uploaded 15 GB of compressed files to an unfamiliar cloud storage service at 3 a.m. The files include customer databases. Which of the following BEST describes this activity?
quizOptions: A) Reconnaissance, the gathering of information about a target before an attack
B) Lateral movement, the spreading from one internal host to others in the network
C) Exfiltration, the unauthorized transfer of data to a location the attacker controls
D) Persistence, the maintaining of access to a system after an initial compromise
detail.explanation: Moving data out of the network to an attacker-controlled location is exfiltration, typically the final goal of a breach. Reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement are earlier or different stages.

definition: A specific piece of code, technique, or method used to take advantage of a vulnerability to cause unintended behavior.
examContext: Exam often presents a proof-of-concept code scenario and asks you to label it as the exploit versus the underlying vulnerability it targets.
analogy: Like the specific lockpick tool used to open an unlocked door, as opposed to the weak lock itself.
relatedTerms: Vulnerability, Zero-day, Threat actor, Buffer overflow

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's red team writes a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages an unpatched buffer overflow vulnerability to gain remote code execution on a test server.
detail.quizQuestion: A security researcher publishes a short script that sends a crafted request to an unpatched web server and opens a remote shell. Separately, the vendor's advisory describes the unchecked input in the server's request parser. Which of the following correctly labels these two items?
quizOptions: A) The script is the exploit, and the unchecked input in the parser is the vulnerability
B) The script is the vulnerability, and the unchecked input in the parser is the exploit
C) The script is the threat actor, and the unchecked input in the parser is the exploit
D) The script is the vulnerability, and the unchecked input in the parser is the risk
detail.explanation: An exploit is the code or technique that takes advantage of a flaw, and the vulnerability is the weakness itself. A threat actor is the person or group, and risk is the likelihood and impact.

items.name: Application
items.detail: Memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOCTOU) and malicious updates.

items.name: Operating system
items.detail: Unpatched or misconfigured OS components and services.

items.name: Web-based
items.detail: SQL injection, XSS and other flaws in web applications.

items.name: Hardware / firmware
items.detail: Flaws in firmware or silicon, plus end-of-life and legacy devices that can no longer be patched.

items.name: Virtualization
items.detail: VM escape (breaking out to the hypervisor or other VMs), resource reuse (data left in reassigned memory or storage), and VM sprawl.

items.name: Cloud-specific
items.detail: Misconfigured storage, over-permissive IAM roles, exposed APIs and weak tenant isolation.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Weaknesses introduced through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider.

items.name: Cryptographic
items.detail: Weak or outdated algorithms, short keys and poor key management.

items.name: Misconfiguration
items.detail: Open permissions, default settings and unnecessary services or protocols.

items.name: Mobile device
items.detail: Side loading and jailbreaking/rooting bypass the platform's security model.

items.name: Zero-day
items.detail: A flaw unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.

definition: An independent examination of an organization's controls by a third party or regulator that provides objective assurance, such as a SOC 2 audit, a regulatory examination or an ISO 27001 certification audit.
examContext: More credible than internal audits and sometimes legally required. It results in an attestation or report.
analogy: The official health inspector, not the owner.
relatedTerms: Internal audit, Self-assessment, Attestation, Compliance

detail.practicalScenario: An independent firm audits a SaaS provider's controls over several months and issues a SOC 2 Type II report that customers can rely on during their own vendor assessments.
detail.quizQuestion: A SaaS provider's customers demand independent assurance that the provider's security controls are effective. Which of the following would BEST provide it?
quizOptions: A) A vulnerability scan that the provider runs against its own production servers
B) An internal audit performed by the provider's own security and compliance team
C) An external audit, such as a SOC 2 report issued by an independent audit firm
D) A self-assessment questionnaire completed by the provider's own management team
detail.explanation: An independent examination by a third party provides objective assurance and is more credible than internal work, which is why customers accept SOC 2 reports. Internal audits, self-assessments and the provider's own scans lack independence.

items.name: Internal
items.detail: Performed by the organization's own staff (an internal audit team or audit committee). Good for readiness and compliance checks; less independent.

items.name: External
items.detail: Performed by an independent third party or a regulator. More objective and credible.

items.name: Self-assessment
items.detail: The organization reviews its own controls against a checklist. Cheap and quick, but the least objective.

items.name: Regulatory examination
items.detail: An audit required by law or a regulator.

items.name: Independent third-party audit
items.detail: An outside auditor attests that controls work (for example a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification).

items.name: Attestation
items.detail: A formal statement from an auditor or responsible party that controls are as described.

definition: A design principle where a system defaults to an unlocked, permissive state upon failure, prioritizing availability and safety over security.
examContext: Commonly tested with fire-exit scenarios where life safety codes require doors to unlock during power failure, even though it reduces security. The objectives contrast it with fail-closed (the same idea as fail secure).
analogy: Like fire doors that automatically unlock in an emergency so people are never trapped inside.
relatedTerms: Fail secure, Availability

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's facility team configures emergency exit doors to unlock automatically during a fire alarm, prioritizing occupant safety even though it temporarily removes access control.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital is configuring electronic locks. The pharmacy door must protect controlled substances, while a corridor exit door on the same circuit must never trap people during a fire. During a power failure, how should each lock behave?
quizOptions: A) The pharmacy lock fails secure and stays locked, and the exit lock fails open and unlocks
B) Both locks fail secure and stay locked, so that controlled substances remain protected at all times
C) The pharmacy lock fails open and unlocks, and the exit lock fails secure and stays locked
D) Both locks fail open and unlock, so that no one is ever trapped in either room
detail.explanation: Fail secure favors security: the lock stays locked, which suits the pharmacy. Fail open favors safety and availability: the lock releases, which life-safety codes require for exits.

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: A design principle where a system defaults to a locked-down, denying state upon failure, prioritizing security over availability. Also called fail-closed.
examContext: The SY0-701 objectives name the pair "fail-open" and "fail-closed", so treat fail secure and fail-closed as the same thing. Exam often contrasts fail secure, where doors lock on power loss, with fail open, where doors unlock on power loss, in physical security scenarios.
analogy: Like a bank vault door that automatically locks shut if the power goes out, keeping intruders from walking in.
relatedTerms: Fail open, Implicit deny, Availability

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures the data center's electronic door locks to remain locked during a power outage, accepting that employees may be briefly inconvenienced in exchange for preventing unauthorized entry.
detail.quizQuestion: A data center's electronic door locks are configured so that, if power to the building is lost, the doors remain locked and require a key to open. Which of the following BEST describes this behavior and a risk of it?
quizOptions: A) Fail open, which locks the room but could prevent anyone from leaving in an emergency
B) Fail open, which keeps the room accessible but exposes the equipment during outages
C) Fail secure, which unlocks the doors but could expose the equipment during an outage
D) Fail secure, which protects the room but could trap people inside during an emergency
detail.explanation: Locks that stay locked on power loss are fail secure (fail closed), which favors security over availability and safety. Fail open unlocks on failure, and the other options mix up the behavior and its consequence.

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: The automatic process of switching to a redundant or standby system, server, or network component the moment the primary one fails or becomes unavailable, minimizing service disruption.
examContext: Know failover is the mechanism or event itself, the switch, while high availability and fault tolerance are the broader goals or properties it helps achieve; exam scenarios describe a primary system going down and traffic automatically shifting to a backup.
analogy: Like a backstage understudy who steps onto the stage the instant the lead actor becomes unable to perform, so the show continues without the audience noticing a gap.
relatedTerms: High availability, Fault tolerance, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures a failover cluster for the company's database so that if the primary database server crashes, the standby replica automatically takes over within seconds, and application connections are redirected with minimal disruption to users.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's primary database server crashes at 2 a.m., and within seconds a standby server takes over without any administrator action. Which of the following terms BEST describes the switch from the primary to the standby server?
quizOptions: A) High availability, the overall design goal of keeping a service accessible
B) Load balancing, the distribution of requests across several active servers
C) Fault tolerance, the ability to keep working without any interruption at all
D) Failover, the automatic switch of service to a redundant standby system
detail.explanation: The act of switching to the standby when the primary fails is failover. High availability is the overall goal, fault tolerance describes components continuing to work through a failure, and load balancing distributes requests among active servers.

items.name: Active-active
items.detail: Every node serves traffic at once: best use of capacity, but losing a node reduces total capacity.

items.name: Active-passive
items.detail: A standby node idles until the active node fails. Simpler and predictable, but the standby capacity is unused.

items.name: Round robin
items.detail: Requests go to servers in rotation. Weighted round robin sends proportionally more to stronger servers.

items.name: Least connections
items.detail: The next request goes to the server with the fewest active connections.

items.name: Source IP hash / persistence
items.detail: The same client keeps going to the same server (sticky sessions), which matters when the server holds session state.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 balancers route on IP and port; Layer 7 balancers route on content such as URL, cookies or headers.

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

definition: A failure to detect a real threat or vulnerability, so a genuine problem is reported as clean.
examContext: More dangerous than a false positive because it creates false assurance. Reduce it with layered detection, up-to-date signatures and more than one scanning method.
analogy: A smoke alarm that stays silent during a real fire.
relatedTerms: False positive, Alert tuning, Vulnerability scanning, IDS

detail.practicalScenario: A signature-based scanner reports a server as clean, but a pentester later exploits an unpatched flaw on it that the scanner missed. The scan result was a false negative.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scanner reports a server as fully patched, but an attacker later exploits a known flaw on that server. The scanner had no credentials for the host and could not inspect its installed software. Which of the following BEST describes the scanner's result and how to reduce it?
quizOptions: A) A false negative, reduced by running credentialed scans and using layered detection
B) A false positive, reduced by tuning the scanner's rules and its alert thresholds
C) A true positive, reduced by blocking the scanner's access to the production network
D) A false negative, reduced by lowering the alert threshold for low-severity findings
detail.explanation: A real flaw that the scanner reported as clean is a false negative, which creates false assurance, and credentialed scans plus layered detection reduce it. A false positive is a nonexistent problem, and lowering thresholds or blocking the scanner does not fix the blind spot.

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.name: Intrusive vs non-intrusive
items.detail: Intrusive scans actively try to exploit and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans only probe and identify.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agent-based: software on the host reports continuously, even for roaming devices. Agentless: the scanner connects over the network.

items.name: Active vs passive
items.detail: Active sends probes; passive listens to traffic and infers what exists without touching it.

items.name: Scan vs pen test
items.detail: A scan is automated and lists KNOWN weaknesses without exploiting them. A pen test is largely manual and exploits weaknesses to prove real impact.

items.name: False positive / false negative
items.detail: False positive: reported but not real (wastes time). False negative: a real flaw that was missed (dangerous).

definition: An alert or scan result that reports a problem that does not actually exist, such as a legitimate file flagged as malware or a vulnerability reported on a system that is already patched.
examContext: Wastes analyst time and causes alert fatigue; reduce it with tuning and credentialed scans. Contrast with a false negative (a real threat that is missed), which is more dangerous.
analogy: A smoke alarm triggered by burnt toast.
relatedTerms: False negative, Alert tuning, Vulnerability scanning, Indicator of compromise

detail.practicalScenario: A vulnerability scanner reports a critical flaw on a web server, but the analyst checks and finds the patch was already installed. The finding is recorded as a false positive and the scan settings are adjusted.
detail.quizQuestion: A SOC analyst spends an hour investigating an alert that flagged a signed backup utility as ransomware. The file is legitimate. Which of the following BEST describes the alert and the long-term fix?
quizOptions: A) A false negative, reduced by adding more signatures for ransomware families
B) A true positive, reduced by blocking the utility on all of the company's endpoints
C) A false positive, reduced by tuning the rule and allowing the legitimate utility
D) A true negative, reduced by increasing the sensitivity of the detection engine
detail.explanation: An alert for something that is not actually a problem is a false positive, and tuning plus an exception for the known utility reduces it. A false negative is a missed threat, a true positive is a real detection, and a true negative is correct silence.

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.name: Intrusive vs non-intrusive
items.detail: Intrusive scans actively try to exploit and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans only probe and identify.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agent-based: software on the host reports continuously, even for roaming devices. Agentless: the scanner connects over the network.

items.name: Active vs passive
items.detail: Active sends probes; passive listens to traffic and infers what exists without touching it.

items.name: Scan vs pen test
items.detail: A scan is automated and lists KNOWN weaknesses without exploiting them. A pen test is largely manual and exploits weaknesses to prove real impact.

items.name: False positive / false negative
items.detail: False positive: reported but not real (wastes time). False negative: a real flaw that was missed (dangerous).

definition: The ability of a system to continue operating properly even when one or more of its components fail, typically achieved through redundancy such as RAID arrays, redundant power supplies, or clustered servers.
examContext: Know fault tolerance is about redundancy at the component level, such as RAID or redundant NICs and power supplies, to prevent a single point of failure, which supports but is distinct from high availability at the system or service level.
analogy: Like a commercial airplane with multiple engines, if one fails mid-flight, the others keep the plane flying safely.
relatedTerms: High availability, Failover, Disaster recovery

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures a RAID 1 mirrored disk array on the critical database server, so that if a single hard drive fails, the system keeps running seamlessly on the remaining mirrored drive with zero data loss or downtime.
detail.quizQuestion: A database server has two power supplies, mirrored disks and two network cards. When one power supply fails, the server keeps running without interruption. Which of the following BEST describes this property?
quizOptions: A) Fault tolerance, achieved by redundant components that remove single points of failure
B) Load balancing, achieved by distributing requests across several active servers
C) Disaster recovery, achieved by restoring systems at an alternate site after an event
D) Failover, achieved when a standby server takes over after the primary server fails
detail.explanation: Redundant power supplies, disks and network cards let the system keep running through a component failure, which is fault tolerance. Failover switches to a standby system, load balancing spreads requests, and disaster recovery restores service after a major event.

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

definition: An arrangement that allows identity information to be trusted and shared across multiple separate organizations or systems, enabling users to access resources across organizational boundaries using a single identity from their home organization.
examContext: Know federation uses standards like SAML and OpenID Connect to let users from one organization, the identity provider, authenticate to services in another, the service provider; a common exam scenario involves partner companies sharing access without creating duplicate accounts.
analogy: Like a university student ID that's also honored at partner universities' libraries, without the student needing to apply for a separate library card at each one.
relatedTerms: Single sign-on, Authentication, Authorization

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan sets up a federation agreement between her company and a key business partner so that the partner's employees can log into a shared project portal using their own corporate credentials, without IT needing to create and manage separate accounts for them.
detail.quizQuestion: Two partner companies want each other's employees to access a shared project portal by using their own corporate credentials, without creating duplicate accounts. The portal trusts the employees' home identity providers. Which of the following BEST describes this arrangement?
quizOptions: A) Password synchronization, in which every system stores the same password hash
B) Provisioning, in which accounts are created in each system for every new user
C) Federation, in which organizations trust each other's identity providers for sign-in
D) Attestation, in which a vendor formally vouches for its compliance with a standard
detail.explanation: Federation lets users authenticate with their home organization's identity, using standards such as SAML or OIDC, to reach another organization's services. Provisioning creates accounts, password synchronization duplicates secrets, and attestation is a statement of compliance.

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: A physical perimeter barrier, typically made of metal or wire and rated by height, that marks a property boundary and deters or delays unauthorized entry onto a site.
examContext: The exam treats fencing as a deterrent and delaying control rather than an absolute barrier, usually paired with other layers like lighting and guards as part of defense in depth.
analogy: Like the wall around a castle: it won't stop a determined attacker forever, but it buys time and discourages casual intruders.
relatedTerms: Bollard, Lighting, Security guard, Defense in depth

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company installs eight-foot perimeter fencing topped with barbed wire around the data center campus, adding a layer of deterrence that works alongside guards and cameras rather than relying on any single control.
detail.quizQuestion: A company is securing a remote equipment yard. It installs an 8-foot fence topped with barbed wire and adds lighting and a guard patrol. A manager says the fence alone is not an absolute barrier. Which of the following BEST describes the role of the fence?
quizOptions: A) It deters and delays intruders, and works best in layers with lighting and guards
B) It corrects damage after a break-in by restoring the yard to its previous state
C) It fully prevents any unauthorized entry, so the other controls are not necessary
D) It detects intruders as they climb it and alerts the guards by itself
detail.explanation: Fencing marks the boundary and deters or delays unauthorized entry, but it is not absolute, so it is combined with lighting and guards as part of defense in depth. It does not detect or correct by itself.

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

definition: Malware that runs in memory and abuses legitimate system tools such as PowerShell or WMI instead of writing executable files to disk, making it hard for signature-based antivirus to detect. Often described as a "living off the land" attack.
examContext: Detect with behavior-based EDR, script logging and restrictions on PowerShell. Persistence may use registry keys or scheduled tasks. It is memory-resident and may vanish at reboot unless persistence is added.
analogy: A burglar who uses the homeowner's own tools and leaves no foreign objects behind.
relatedTerms: Malware, Memory injection, Persistence, EDR, Rootkit

detail.practicalScenario: An analyst sees PowerShell spawned from a Word macro and connecting to an unknown server, yet no malicious file exists on disk. EDR flags the behavior and isolates the host.
detail.quizQuestion: An EDR alert shows that PowerShell launched from a Word document is running encoded commands that load code directly into memory. No new executable files were written to disk, and the antivirus scan is clean. Which of the following BEST describes this malware?
quizOptions: A) A logic bomb stored as a script file on disk that triggers on a specific date
B) A boot sector virus, which infects the master boot record and loads at startup
C) A rootkit installed as a kernel driver file that hides processes from the user
D) Fileless malware, which runs in memory and abuses legitimate tools like PowerShell
detail.explanation: Memory-resident code that abuses legitimate tools like PowerShell and writes no executable file is fileless malware, a living-off-the-land technique that signature antivirus misses. A boot sector virus, a rootkit driver and a logic bomb script all involve files on disk.

definition: A network security device or software that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on predetermined security rules, acting as a barrier between trusted internal networks and untrusted external networks.
examContext: Know firewall types such as packet-filtering, stateful, and next-generation, and their placement at network perimeters; exam scenarios often ask which rule to add or modify to block or allow specific traffic.
analogy: Like a security checkpoint at a building entrance that checks everyone's ID against a list of rules before allowing them in or out.
relatedTerms: Stateful inspection, Packet filtering, Proxy server, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the perimeter firewall to block all inbound traffic except HTTPS on port 443 to the web server, significantly reducing the organization's exposed attack surface.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's web server in the DMZ should accept HTTPS from anywhere, but only administrators on the management network should be able to reach its SSH service. Which firewall rule set BEST implements this?
quizOptions: A) Allow TCP 22 from the management subnet only, then allow all other traffic through
B) Place a deny all rule first, then allow TCP 443 and TCP 22 from any source address
C) Allow TCP 443 and TCP 22 from any source address, then deny all other traffic
D) Allow 443 from anywhere and 22 from the management subnet only, then deny all
detail.explanation: The rules permit HTTPS broadly, restrict SSH to the management subnet and end with a deny all. Allowing SSH from anywhere defeats the restriction, a deny all rule placed first blocks everything, and ending with allow all removes the default deny.

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

definition: A backup that copies all selected data regardless of whether it has changed. It takes the longest and uses the most storage, but gives the fastest and simplest restore because everything is in one set.
examContext: Compare with incremental (only changes since the last backup) and differential (changes since the last full). Full backups are the base for all other types.
analogy: Photocopying the whole book every time instead of just the changed pages.
relatedTerms: Incremental backup, Differential backup, Backup, Snapshot

detail.practicalScenario: Every Sunday the admin runs a full backup of the file server. On a restore, only that single set is needed, so recovery is quick and simple, though the backup window is long.
detail.quizQuestion: A company can only run backups on Sundays because of network load, and it wants the fastest and simplest possible restore if a server fails. It has plenty of storage and a long backup window. Which backup type BEST fits?
quizOptions: A) Incremental backup, because it copies only the changes since the previous backup
B) Differential backup, because it copies the changes since the last full backup
C) Full backup, because everything is in one set for a quick and simple restore
D) Snapshot, because it keeps a copy of the data that is stored on the same volume
detail.explanation: A full backup copies everything, takes the longest and uses the most storage, but a restore needs just one set. Incremental and differential backups save time and space but need more sets to restore, and a snapshot on the same volume is not an independent backup.

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: A structured comparison between an organization's current security controls or posture and a desired target state, such as a framework, regulation, or best-practice baseline, used to identify specific deficiencies that need remediation.
examContext: Gap analysis is tested as a governance and compliance activity typically performed before adopting a new framework or after an audit, producing a prioritized list of missing or weak controls; don't confuse it with a tabletop exercise, which tests response procedures rather than compares current state to a target.
analogy: Like comparing a home inspection report against a target checklist to see exactly which repairs are still needed before the house meets code.
relatedTerms: Governance, Risk register, Due diligence, Risk management

detail.practicalScenario: Maria performs a gap analysis comparing the company's existing controls against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, producing a report that identifies missing encryption standards and outdated incident response procedures that must be addressed.
detail.quizQuestion: A company plans to adopt the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. Before spending money, the security manager wants a list of which of the framework's outcomes the company already meets and which it does not, ranked by priority. Which of the following activities BEST provides this?
quizOptions: A) A gap analysis that compares the current controls with the target framework
B) A business impact analysis that ranks business processes by the cost of downtime
C) A tabletop exercise that tests the response procedures with a simulated incident
D) A penetration test that attempts to exploit weaknesses in the production systems
detail.explanation: A gap analysis compares the current state with a target such as a framework or regulation and produces a prioritized list of missing or weak controls. A tabletop tests response, a penetration test exploits weaknesses, and a BIA ranks processes by downtime impact.

definition: A control that uses GPS, Wi-Fi or IP location to define a virtual boundary and trigger an action when a device enters or leaves it, such as blocking access, locking a phone or sending an alert. Also used as a geographic restriction on data access.
examContext: Appears in MDM policies (disable the camera inside a facility), conditional access (deny logins from outside the country) and data protection (geographic restrictions). Weakness: GPS or IP spoofing and VPNs.
analogy: An invisible electric-fence line around a property that sounds an alarm when crossed.
relatedTerms: Data sovereignty, Multifactor authentication, Biometrics, MDM

detail.practicalScenario: A company's MDM policy turns off the camera on any phone while it is inside the research lab and blocks access to the CRM from outside the country. Both rules rely on location boundaries.
detail.quizQuestion: A company issues tablets to field technicians. It wants the tablets to lock and send an alert if they leave the country, and to disable their cameras inside the company's research lab. Which of the following BEST provides this?
quizOptions: A) Full-disk encryption that uses a key stored in the tablets' trusted module
B) A VPN with split tunneling enabled for traffic that goes to the internet
C) Geofencing policies that use location to trigger actions in the MDM platform
D) A captive portal that requires acceptance of terms on public Wi-Fi networks
detail.explanation: Geofencing uses GPS, Wi-Fi or IP location to define a virtual boundary and trigger actions such as locking a device or disabling the camera, and MDM policies apply it. A VPN, disk encryption and a captive portal do not respond to location.

definition: Placing data centers, backups or recovery sites in separate regions so a single local disaster, outage or regional event cannot take down all systems or copies of data.
examContext: Part of resilience and site considerations. Distance should exceed the likely disaster radius, but dispersion can conflict with data sovereignty requirements.
analogy: Keeping copies of important documents in different cities so one fire or flood cannot destroy them all.
relatedTerms: Hot site, Disaster recovery, Data sovereignty, Platform diversity

detail.practicalScenario: A company stores its backups in a data center 800 km from its headquarters so a regional hurricane cannot destroy both the primary systems and their copies.
detail.quizQuestion: A company hosts its primary data center and its backup data center 20 miles apart in the same coastal city. A hurricane takes both offline for a week. Which of the following changes BEST prevents a single regional event from taking down both sites?
quizOptions: A) Add a second generator and a larger UPS to the existing backup data center
B) Locate the backup site in a different region, beyond the likely disaster radius
C) Move the backup site to a floor above the primary servers in the same building
D) Replicate the data between the two sites more often so that less data is lost
detail.explanation: Geographic dispersion places sites far enough apart that one regional event cannot affect both. Generators and more frequent replication do not help when both sites are offline, and putting the backup in the same building makes the shared risk worse.

definition: The overall framework of policies, roles, and processes an organization uses to direct and control its information security program.
examContext: SY0-701 tests governance as the umbrella over policies, standards, procedures, and guidelines; expect questions on who sets direction versus who implements it.
analogy: Like a company's constitution, which sets the rules everyone else must operate within.
relatedTerms: Risk management, Due care, Due diligence, Data classification

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's executive team establishes a formal security governance committee that approves all new policies, ensuring IT security decisions align with business and regulatory requirements.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's board of directors wants to ensure that its security program has clear direction. It asks who sets the policies and standards, who is accountable for them and who carries them out. Which of the following BEST describes the framework that answers these questions?
quizOptions: A) Penetration testing, the controlled attack on systems to find weaknesses
B) Incident response, the process of handling a security event after it occurs
C) Vulnerability management, the cycle of finding and patching weaknesses in systems
D) Governance, the framework of policies, roles and processes that directs the program
detail.explanation: Governance is the overall framework of policies, roles and processes that directs and controls the security program, including who sets direction and who implements it. The other options are operational activities within a program.

items.name: Fines
items.detail: Monetary penalties set by regulators (GDPR is the best-known example).

items.name: Sanctions
items.detail: Formal restrictions or penalties, including legal action or being barred from certain activity.

items.name: Reputational damage
items.detail: Loss of customer trust and negative press.

items.name: Loss of license
items.detail: Losing the right to operate, handle payment cards, or practice in a regulated field.

items.name: Contractual impacts
items.detail: Breach of contract, terminated agreements and lost business.

variants.title: Policy, standard, procedure and guideline compared

items.name: Policy
items.detail: A high-level management statement of WHAT must be done and why. Broad, mandatory, and rarely changed (for example the Acceptable Use Policy).

items.name: Standard
items.detail: Specific, MANDATORY requirements that support a policy (passwords of 14+ characters, AES-256 for data at rest).

items.name: Procedure
items.detail: Step-by-step instructions on HOW to carry out a task (an onboarding checklist, a restore runbook).

items.name: Guideline
items.detail: Recommended best practice. ADVISORY and flexible, not mandatory.

items.name: Baseline
items.detail: The minimum secure configuration that systems must meet (see secure baseline).

items.name: Common policies
items.detail: Acceptable use, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management, password, remote access, data retention and onboarding/offboarding.

items.name: Boards
items.detail: Set strategy and oversee risk at the top of the organization.

items.name: Committees
items.detail: Cross-functional groups such as a security steering committee or a Change Advisory Board (CAB).

items.name: Government entities
items.detail: Regulators and agencies that set legal requirements at local, regional, national and global levels.

items.name: Centralized
items.detail: One authority sets policy for everyone. Consistent, but slower and less tailored.

items.name: Decentralized
items.detail: Business units set their own policy. Flexible, but risks inconsistency.

items.name: Monitoring and revision
items.detail: Policies must be reviewed regularly and updated when laws, threats or the business change.

definition: A predefined constraint built into an automated or orchestrated process that prevents a script, pipeline, or system from taking an action outside of approved, safe boundaries, even if instructed to.
examContext: Appears in the automation and orchestration exam objectives; know guard rails as automatic policy enforcement built into scripts and pipelines that stop an unsafe action, such as an overly broad deletion, before it can execute.
analogy: Like the physical guard rails along a mountain road that keep a car from driving off the edge even if the driver makes a mistake.
relatedTerms: Change management, Governance, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: Chen builds a guard rail into the company's automated remediation script so that it will never delete more than a small, defined number of accounts in a single run, preventing a buggy automation rule from accidentally mass-deleting production user accounts during an unattended overnight job.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud automation script is given a command that would delete every storage bucket in a production account. The orchestration platform blocks the action because it violates a policy that limits deletions to non-production resources. Which of the following BEST describes this protection?
quizOptions: A) A honeytoken, which is a fake credential that signals unauthorized use
B) A guard rail, which prevents automated actions outside approved boundaries
C) A backout plan, which is a procedure for reversing a change that has failed
D) A baseline, which is a documented standard set of secure configuration settings
detail.explanation: A guard rail is a predefined constraint in automation that stops an unsafe action, such as an overly broad deletion, before it executes. A honeytoken detects misuse, a baseline is a reference configuration, and a backout plan reverses a failed change.

items.name: User provisioning
items.detail: Automatically create, change and remove accounts as people join, move and leave.

items.name: Resource provisioning
items.detail: Spin up servers, networks and cloud resources from code (infrastructure as code).

items.name: Guard rails
items.detail: Automated limits that stop risky actions before they happen.

items.name: Security groups
items.detail: Automatically apply and adjust network access rules.

items.name: Ticket creation and escalation
items.detail: Alerts automatically open tickets and escalate them if unanswered.

items.name: Enabling / disabling services and access
items.detail: Quickly turn services or accounts on or off, such as disabling a compromised account.

items.name: Continuous integration and testing
items.detail: Automatically build and test code on every change to catch problems early.

items.name: Integrations and APIs
items.detail: Connect tools so they share data and trigger each other (SOAR playbooks).

definition: An attacker motivated by political, social or ideological beliefs who uses attacks such as website defacement, DDoS and data leaks to promote a cause or embarrass a target.
examContext: Moderate skill and resources; the motive is philosophical or political belief. Typical actions: defacement, DDoS, doxing and leaking documents. Anonymous is the usual example.
analogy: A protester with a keyboard instead of a picket sign.
relatedTerms: Threat actor, Nation-state actor, Organized crime, Unskilled attacker

detail.practicalScenario: After a controversial announcement, a group floods an agency's website with traffic and defaces its homepage with a protest message. No data is sold; the goal is attention for the cause.
detail.quizQuestion: A group defaces a mining company's website with environmental slogans, launches a DDoS attack against its portal and leaks internal memos online to embarrass the company. The group has moderate skills and makes no financial demands. Which type of threat actor is MOST likely responsible?
quizOptions: A) A nation-state actor, which is motivated by long-term strategic espionage
B) An insider threat, which is motivated by personal grievances or financial gain
C) Hacktivists, who use attacks to promote a political or ideological cause
D) An organized crime group, which is motivated by large and repeatable profits
detail.explanation: Defacement, DDoS and leaks to promote a cause without financial demands are typical of hacktivists. Organized crime seeks profit, nation-states pursue espionage or strategic aims, and insiders act from inside the organization.

definition: The process of reducing a system's attack surface by disabling unnecessary services, closing unused ports, removing default accounts, applying secure configurations, and installing patches.
examContext: Know hardening as a broad proactive category covering OS, application, and network device configuration; exam scenarios often list specific hardening actions, such as disabling services or changing default passwords, as the correct way to reduce risk.
analogy: Like reinforcing a house by locking unused doors, boarding up unnecessary windows, and removing spare keys left under the doormat.
relatedTerms: Baseline configuration, Patch management, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: Chen hardens a newly deployed server by disabling unused network services, renaming the default administrator account, and removing sample applications, reducing the number of potential entry points before the server goes into production.
detail.quizQuestion: A new Linux web server was built from the vendor's default image and goes live tomorrow. A scan shows FTP and Telnet listening, a default administrator account with a published password, and SSH open to all networks. Which of the following actions would BEST reduce the server's attack surface before go-live?
quizOptions: A) Place the server behind a load balancer and add a second web server to handle failover during outages
B) Disable the unneeded services, change or remove the default account, and restrict SSH to the management network
C) Install antivirus software on the server and schedule weekly full-system scans with automatic signature updates
D) Enable nightly full backups of the web content and database and keep a copy at an offsite location
detail.explanation: Hardening removes what an attacker could use: unneeded services and open ports, default credentials and unrestricted management access. Antivirus, backups and load balancing add detection, recovery or availability but leave the exposed services and default account in place.

items.name: Workstations and endpoints
items.detail: Install endpoint protection, enable a host firewall, patch, encrypt the disk, remove unnecessary software and bloatware, and run as a standard user.

items.name: Servers
items.detail: Minimal role-specific installs, disable unneeded services, patch, least privilege, logging and a secure baseline.

items.name: Switches and routers
items.detail: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH rather than Telnet, SNMPv3, port security, ACLs and firmware updates.

items.name: Cloud infrastructure
items.detail: Least-privilege IAM, MFA, no public storage buckets, encryption, logging and configuration scanning.

items.name: Mobile devices
items.detail: MDM policies, passcodes, encryption, remote wipe, app allow lists, and no sideloading.

items.name: IoT and embedded
items.detail: Change default credentials, update firmware, isolate on their own VLAN, and disable unused features.

items.name: ICS / SCADA / RTOS
items.detail: Segmentation or an air gap, strict physical security, monitoring and compensating controls, because patching is often impractical.

items.name: Common steps
items.detail: Change default passwords, disable unnecessary ports and protocols, remove unnecessary software, patch, and install endpoint protection.

items.name: Segmentation
items.detail: Split the network so a compromise cannot spread freely.

items.name: Access control (ACLs and permissions)
items.detail: Restrict who and what can reach a resource.

items.name: Application allow list
items.detail: Only approved programs may run; everything else is blocked by default.

items.name: Isolation
items.detail: Separate or quarantine a risky or infected system from the rest of the environment.

items.name: Patching
items.detail: Fix known vulnerabilities.

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Protect data confidentiality at rest and in transit.

items.name: Monitoring
items.detail: Detect problems early through logging, SIEM and alerts.

items.name: Least privilege
items.detail: Grant only the access needed to do the job.

items.name: Configuration enforcement
items.detail: Automatically keep systems in line with the secure baseline.

items.name: Decommissioning
items.detail: Securely retire systems that are no longer needed, wiping data.

definition: A one-way mathematical function that converts input data of any size into a fixed-length output, used to verify integrity since the same input always produces the same output and the process cannot be reversed to recover the original data.
examContext: SY0-701 emphasizes hashing algorithms like SHA-256 for integrity verification and password storage; remember hashing is one-way, unlike encryption which is reversible with a key.
analogy: Like a fingerprint of a document, unique to the content, but you can't reconstruct the document from the fingerprint alone.
relatedTerms: Salting, Key stretching, Digital signature, Integrity

detail.practicalScenario: Chen computes a SHA-256 hash of a downloaded software installer and compares it to the hash posted on the vendor's website to confirm the file was not corrupted or tampered with during download.
detail.quizQuestion: A web application stores user passwords. The security team wants a method that lets the application check a submitted password without ever being able to recover the original passwords from the stored data. Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?
quizOptions: A) Store each password encoded with Base64, so that it is not shown in plain text
B) Store a salted hash of each password, which is one-way and cannot be reversed
C) Store each password encrypted with AES, so that the application can decrypt it
D) Store each password in a file that is protected with a strong access control list
detail.explanation: A salted hash is a one-way function: the application hashes the submitted password and compares it, and the original cannot be recovered. AES can be decrypted, Base64 is only an encoding, and an access control list still leaves passwords in readable form.

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

items.name: MD5
items.detail: 128-bit digest. Broken: practical collision attacks exist, so never use it where security matters. Still seen for quick, non-security file checks.

items.name: SHA-1
items.detail: 160-bit digest. Deprecated: collisions were demonstrated in 2017. Browsers and CAs no longer accept SHA-1 certificates.

items.name: SHA-2 (SHA-256 / SHA-512)
items.detail: The current workhorse family (224/256/384/512-bit digests). SHA-256 is the most common choice for file integrity, certificates and signatures.

items.name: SHA-3
items.detail: Standardized in 2015 using a different internal design (Keccak) from SHA-2. Not a replacement forced by SHA-2 weakness; it is a structurally different fallback.

items.name: RIPEMD
items.detail: Open-design 160-bit hash (RIPEMD-160), an alternative to the SHA family; best known for use in Bitcoin address generation.

items.name: bcrypt / PBKDF2 / Argon2
